title: Beyond Resistance Detection: Genotypic Determinants of Drug-Resistant Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Their Association with Treatment Outcomes in Rural South Africa
content: Background: Understanding the relationship between genotypic drug resistance and tuberculosis (TB) treatment outcomes requires reliable molecular testing results and complete clinical records. In resource-constrained settings, incomplete laboratory and treatment documentation may limit the interpretation of genotype–outcome associations and weaken clinical governance. This pilot study examined resistance-associated mutation profiles, their associations with recorded treatment outcomes, and the completeness of routinely collected molecular and clinical data in rural Eastern Cape, South Africa. Methods: A retrospective analysis of 456 routinely collected TB patient records from 2023 to 2024 was conducted. Available first-line and second-line molecular resistance results and recorded treatment outcomes were summarised. Favourable treatment outcomes were compared across resistance profiles, and multivariable logistic regression was used to explore associations between mutation categories and favourable outcomes among complete cases. Results: Treatment outcomes were documented for 380 of 456 records (83.3%), whereas first- and second-line molecular results were available for 207 (45.4%) and 181 (39.7%) records, respectively. Only 164 records contained paired first line and second-line molecular results, of which 139 also had recorded treatment outcomes. Favourable outcomes occurred in 68 of 85 patients (80.0%) with no mutations detected in the assessed targets, 28 of 41 (68.3%) with first-line resistance-associated mutations only, and eight of 13 (61.5%) with combined first-line and second-line mutations. Although favourable outcomes decreased numerically across these categories, the overall comparison was not statistically significant (p = 0.187). Among 122 complete cases included in multivariable analysis, neither first-line mutations alone (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 0.77; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.23–2.59) nor combined first-line and second-line mutations (aOR 0.57; 95% CI 0.12–2.62) demonstrated statistically significant associations with favourable outcomes. Conclusions: Resistance-associated mutation profiles showed numerical differences in recorded treatment outcomes, but the evidence was insufficient to establish statistically significant associations. Incomplete molecular testing results and treatment-outcome documentation substantially restricted integrated genotype–outcome analysis. Strengthening laboratory–clinical data linkage, standardised outcome recording and routine data-quality monitoring may improve the interpretability of DR-TB surveillance and support evidence-informed clinical governance in resource-constrained settings.
